s.h:
Set in and around the vast Galactic Co-Prosperity Sphere, Epic Warpath is an immersive and exciting game of futuristic battles fought on alien worlds.

All of this is represented by collections of highly detailed Mantic models and is played out on your tabletop with evocative terrain, special dice and tokens to keep track of the action. A game of Epic Warpath is usually played between two players, each controlling an army of highly trained (or degenerate) warriors and futuristic vehicles, all vying for control of strategic objectives. Games involving more players and/or more armies are possible, but they require additional rules and so will be treated separately in their own expansions or articles.

s.t: What you need to Play Epic Warpath

s.h: Each player will need suitable Mantic models to assemble their army. Each army could range from a mix of infantry and vehicles to vast hordes of troops with walker and flier support - there really is no limit!

Epic Warpath is normally played on a 6’x4’ (72” x 48”) table space. For truly epic games, larger table spaces can be used to accommodate all the models and scenery you are using. Likewise, for smaller games, you can play on a smaller area

Epic Warpath uses 8-sided dice (abbreviated to D8) for most rolls in the game. Once rolled, the result is the number showing on the top face – just like on a standard six-sided die.

For most rolls in the game, you roll the required number of D8s and then compare the scores to the appropriate models’ or weapons’ statistic (stat). For example a value of 4+ for a Shoot stat means scores of 4 or more are successes. Thus, all dice that equal or exceed the stat value are successes, and all that are less than the target number are failures. If a base has a stat value of “–“ then no dice are rolled and therefore no successes can be achieved.

For example, Paul rolls four D8s to shoot using his Unit’s Shoot value of 6+. He rolls a 3, 5, 6 and 7 scoring 2 successes.

Sometimes a D4 or D2 may be required. In such cases, simply roll a D8 and determine the result using the table below:

D8 Roll D4 Result D2 Result
1-2 1 1
3-4 2 1
5-6 3 2
7-8 4 2

Some dice rolls are modified by adding to, or subtracting from the number rolled, making a success more or less easy to achieve. In all cases a natural roll (regardless of modifiers) of 1 is always a failure.

Modifiers are cumulative, so two modifiers that are both -1, result in a total modifier of -2 to the score on the dice for example; and -1, -1 and +1 would result in a final modifier of -1.

Returning to our previous example, if Paul’s roll suffered a -1 modifier, his dice would have scored 2, 4, 5 and 6, resulting in only one success. If the modifier was +1 his results would have been 4, 6, 7 and 8 and three dice would have achieved the 6 or more he required, and so would all be successes.

Sometimes a rule will state that there is a maximum modifier that can apply. In such cases, apply all modifiers first and then apply the maximum “cap” to the result.

Exploding 8s

For some rolls in the game a mechanism called Exploding 8s is used. This means that for each natural result of 8 in the roll (that is also a success), another bonus die can be rolled to see if a further success is achieved. It’s possible to keep rolling 8s and to keep getting bonus dice!

The rules will state when the Exploding 8! mechanic applies to a roll.

Bonus dice can be re-rolled just like any other dice if permitted. Finish accumulating and rolling any bonus dice before any re-rolling.

e.g. five dice are rolled with the Sustained Attack keyword, requiring scores of 5 or more to be a success. The results are 2, 4, 5, 6 and 8. Three results are successes and a bonus die is rolled which scores another 8 - another success and so a further bonus die is rolled. This time a 3 is rolled and the sequence stops. Overall, four successes were rolled.

Some Keywords and orders will allow you to re-roll dice to improve your chances of a success, or force your opponent to re-roll successful dice rolls. In all cases, you may only ever re-roll each die once – you cannot re-roll a re-roll, even if the source of the re-roll is different. If both players have rules allowing them to make rerolls to the same roll, the player whose Turn it is, makes their re-rolls first
Throughout the game, whenever a number is divided and the result is not a whole number, always round the result up. For example, 3.5 would round up to 4.

Some weapons or effects are unpredictable. To represent this, Epic Warpath uses a special Targeting Die, which indicates direction using the natural points of the die, distance (3,3,4,5,6), and ‘ON TARGET’ symbols (x3). The Targeting Die is 8-sided and is read just like a normal die, using the face-up side as the result. The point to use for direction is marked with a chevron/arrow.

To play Epic Warpath you will need a set of Command Dice. These 6-sided Command Dice are coloured black, orange or green, which represent the capability of progressively more powerful commanders or units. Each die face is either blank or has a number of energy swords on them. The number of energy swords rolled is the number of Command Points scored for that die.

There are a number of tokens, counters and markers used in games of Epic Warpath, for tracking things like Unit Actions and Pinning. What these look like and when to use them are described within the rules.

Groups of models that are selected within an army and which move and fight together are called Units. All the models within a Unit will be mounted on one or more Bases.

All models in Epic Warpath, except some vehicles, are mounted on round bases. A Base could represent a single walker or a small squad of infantry models, for example. One or more Bases are formed into Units. Bases in a Unit operate together during the game.

Vehicles without Bases

If a vehicle is supplied and used without a base, consider the footprint of its hull to be its “Base”. Some people prefer to create their own bases for these vehicles. This is fine, but such scratch-built bases should not be much larger than the vehicle itself. Measure from this base as normal.

Base Contact

A Base is in base contact with something when it is physically touching it (such as an enemy base, building, Objective etc.). When two Bases are touching, they are in base contact.
Several Keywords and effects in the game may require use of a Status Marker. These are generic tokens in various colours for you to use as you wish.

All Units in Epic Warpath have a profile of statistics or ‘stats’ which show how effective the Bases in the Unit are at moving, shooting, assaulting and surviving in a combat zone. In addition, the height of the Bases in a Unit, their Keywords and weaponry are all included in the profile.

Some Units may be so poor at doing something they will be effectively unable to do it at all! Such Units will have a stat value of “-” where appropriate. Here is an example of a Unit profile for Enforcer Jet Bikes, made of 6 Bases.

Unit Name: Each Unit is identified by its title.

Bases: The number of Bases the Unit starts with. This is indicated next to the Unit’s name in brackets. For example (6) means the Unit starts with 6 Bases

Type: The type of Unit is used for a number of rules in the game. Types include Infantry, Heavy Infantry, Vehicle, Bike, Walker and Super-heavy. Units listed as Command, will also have a type in Brackets. For example Command (Infantry), or Command (Vehicle). For the purposes of the rules, they are both types.

Speed (SP): How far a Unit can move in inches, given as two values (n/n – Advance/Sprint). The first number is used to represent the Unit’s basic Advance movement. The second number is used when the Unit Sprints.

Shoot (SH): The ability of a Unit to fire ranged weapons accurately. A Unit with a stat value of “-” cannot Shoot.

Assault (AS): The skill or strength of a Unit in handto-hand combat. If a Unit has a stat value of “-” it will roll no dice to attack in an Assault.

Armour (AR): The armour, or toughness of a model when potentially taking damage.

Save (SV): This represents supernatural foresight, plain luck, uncanny reflexes, shielding technology, or any other way to evade damage.

Height (HT): The Unit’s Height value. This value is used primarily to determine Line of Sight and Cover.

Unit Strength (US): These values represent the ability of the Unit to take and hold an Objective. Units with higher US values will win out if an Objective is contested. Typically, infantry will have better US than bikes or vehicles, representing their ability to bed in and lock down an area. The value is usually expressed as n/n (e.g. 4/2 or 3/1). A Unit uses the first number as its US value until it has lost half or more of its Bases, after which it immediately uses the second number. See page 55 for more on Objective scoring.

Points (PTS): The cost to purchase the Unit when building your army. The points cost includes a number of Bases and standard equipment. PTS cost is also used to determine the winner in some Scenarios.

Weapon Stats: The Ranged and Assault (range A) weaponry of the Bases within the Unit, and their Keywords. Where Attack Dice (ADice) are listed, this is the number of dice that a weapon gets for each Base in the Unit.

Keywords: Some Units and weapons will have special abilities that allow them certain advantages, or disadvantages, in the game. These Keywords may be for the Unit as a whole or for individual weapons within the Unit. This will be clearly shown in the Unit profile.

For example, in the profile opposite, all the Bases in the Unit have the Anti-Grav Keyword, and their Dominator Rifles have the Sustained Attack Keyword.

Nerve is a single value that is set for an Army as a whole, instead of an individual Unit. If a Unit has to make a Nerve test for any reason, roll a single D8 and compare the result to the Army Nerve value. If the result equals or beats the Army Nerve value, the test is passed. Otherwise, it is a failure.

In a game of Epic Warpath, you and your opponent each take control of an Army of soldiers to play an exciting battle game. Once the battlefield has been set up with terrain and any objectives, your chosen Scenario will tell you how to deploy your Units and how to achieve victory!

Friendly Elements: If a rule refers to friendly Units/Bases, this means all Units and Bases in your army.

Enemy Elements: If a rule refers to enemy Units/Bases, this means all Units and Bases in your opponent’s army.

Neutral Elements: If a Scenario requires the use of third party elements, these are considered neutral and are classed as enemy elements for both players.

All Units and Bases are In Play if they are currently placed on the gaming table, including Flying Units, but also includes Units within transports and buildings (even if the actual models are currently placed to one side). Units and Bases that are currently in Reserve (awaiting deployment), or that have been destroyed, are not In Play.

A tape measure marked in inches is required to play Epic Warpath in order to determine how far Bases move or shoot etc. Measurement between Bases, Objectives, and range to targets is always taken as the distance between the closest points on the two elements involved (e.g. base edge to base edge, rather than centre to centre). You can measure to check distances or range at any time.

Line of Sight (LOS) is determined by using a top-down view, looking down on the table as if from a drone or satellite. Often whether Bases and Units have LOS to a target is obvious, but the top-down approach makes it clear when there is any doubt.

All Bases have a 360 degree arc of sight – so they can see all around them.

All Bases have a 360 degree arc of sight – so they can see all around themTo determine if a Unit has LOS to a target, draw a straight, imaginary line from any part of a Base in the friendly Unit to any Base in the target enemy Unit. Bases from the friendly Unit checking for LOS, or target Unit, and any Bases with the Fly Keyword, do not block LOS. Any Bases, or gaps between Bases, in other intervening Units will block LOS up to that Unit’s height. Players should check for LOS from each Base in a Unit, as only some may be able to see a target (or not all the Bases in an enemy Unit may be visible).

If a Base checking for LOS can draw an uninterrupted line to all parts of an enemy Base, then LOS is considered to be Clear

If it’s impossible to draw this imaginary line to any part of an enemy Base, without it being interrupted by terrain or Bases with a Height equal or greater than both target and the Base drawing LOS, then LOS is Blocked.

LOS from a Base to the enemy is considered Partially Blocked if:

  • The imaginary line can be drawn to some, but not all of the enemy base, because it is obscured by something that blocks LOS.
  • The line passes over a Base or terrain feature that is lower than both target and shooter (e.g. firing over an intervening wall or shorter Unit).
  • The line passes over a Base or terrain feature that is equal in height to either the target or shooter, and lower than the other.

An enemy Unit can be seen so long as LOS is either Clear or Partially Blocked. When LOS is Partially Blocked, the enemy Unit is often said to be In Cover.

The Benefit of Elevation

Units can ignore any intervening terrain elements or Units that are 3 or more Height levels lower than they are.

For example, a Unit in a solid building is Height 5 and so can ignore (see clearly over) intervening elements of Height 2 or less.

Large Targets

Conversely, targets that themselves are 3 Height levels or taller than intervening terrain or Units, cannot claim LOS is Blocked or Partially Blocked by those elements.

For example, a Height 2 Unit can ignore a Height 1 barricade when shooting up at a Unit in a Height 6 building.

A game of Epic Warpath is played over a series of Rounds, which are each conducted in a number of Phases. Within each Phase each player will alternate taking Turns to activate their Units, one at a time, until both players have completed activating all the eligible Units in their army. Once one of the players has completed all their possible activations in a phase, the other player then completes all of theirs.

The Scenario being played will determine the number of Rounds in a game, together with terrain set-up, troops deployment, victory conditions and so on; see the Scenario Section on page 51.

Each Round in Epic Warpath is played in the same order through a sequence of phases as follows.

  1. Command Phase
  2. Movement Phase
  3. Overwatch Phase
  4. Combat Phase
  5. End Phase

Command Phase

In the Command Phase, players perform the following in order.

  1. Roll for Command Points
  2. Assign Action Tokens
  3. Roll for Initiative
  4. Reveal Hidden Action Tokens

Movement Phase

Units that have been assigned Sprint or Advance Action Tokens take it in turn to move in this Phase. Units which will engage the enemy in Assault, swap their Sprint token for a Combat Token, otherwise the token is simply removed once the Sprint is complete. Units with Advance tokens perform any movement and then swap them for Combat Tokens.

Overwatch Phase

Units with Overwatch Action Tokens take it in turns to shoot at the enemy using any ranged weapons they have. Once a Unit has fired, its token is removed.

Combat Phase

Units with Combat Tokens take it in turn to either fight in close combat (Assault) with enemy troops, or shoot with ranged weapons. As each Unit completes its action, its token is removed.

End Phase

Any special rules which take place in the End Phase are carried out. Players roll for Pin marker removal. Players then check the Scenario conditions to see if someone has achieved victory. If not, the game continues and the next Round starts with the Command Phase.
In the Command Phase, players perform the following in order.
Each player rolls three black Command Dice, plus any additional Command Dice generated by Tactician units (see page 50), to generate their own Pool of Command Points.
The three possible Action Tokens to place in this phase are:

First of all, players place the following Tokens, face up next to the relevant units, as described below.

  • Engaged Units: Units that are engaged in Assault with each other from a previous Round must be given Combat Tokens instead of one of the Action Tokens listed above.
  • Pinned Units: Unengaged units that start the Round with a Pin marker must be given an Advance Token. Units that are both Pinned and Engaged receive no tokens of any kind.
  • Command Units: Unengaged Command Units that are not Pinned must be given both a Sprint and an Overwatch Token.

Simultaneously, both players select the Action Token they want for each remaining unit they have In Play (and Reserves that will be entering the battle this Round, see page 58) that has not yet received a Token (i.e. that was not included in the Mandatory Tokens listed above). These Action Tokens should be placed face down next to the Unit receiving the Token.

Note that Units aboard transports are not assigned any Token, but are assumed to have the same Token as their transports (see page 41).

Unless a Scenario instructs otherwise, both players roll a D8 in the first Command Phase and the winner has the Initiative for the Round. Re-roll ties. In each subsequent Command Phase, players roll for Initiative again to see which one has it for that Round. If a tie is rolled, the player that didn’t have the Initiative in the previous Round wins.

The player with the Initiative for the Round should take the Initiative Token as a reminder.

For the rest of the Round, the player with the Initiative Token can decide which players goes first in each phase.

In addition, whenever two rules are triggered at the same time, the player with the Initiative can decide in which order all of these simultaneously triggered rules are resolved (unless the rules state otherwise).

For example, imagine a Unit is assaulting another and it has a rule like a Strategic order which can be triggered ‘when assaulting an enemy’. Similarly, the defender could have a rule that can be triggered ‘when assaulted’. The player with the Initiative decides which player must trigger their rule first.

Both players turn over and reveal all the hidden Action Tokens they gave to their Units. If a player has forgotten to place a Token on a Unit, it is now given a Combat Token. Note that this is the last chance for a unit to receive Action Tokens. If you forget to do so and you start the Movement phase, then any forgotten Units will have no action for this Round.

Soldiers will work best if properly led and organised which involves solid leadership and good orders. To simulate this, we use Command Points and Orders to represent your ability to get the most from your army.

In this example, sam has rolled three black command dice plus an orange one for a command unit with the tactician (orange) keyword. After re-rolling one die to try for a better result, the fInal total is 5 command points to spend in the coming round.

At the start of each Round both players create their Command Dice Pool by taking three BLACK Command Dice. Additional dice of the appropriate colour (BLACK, ORANGE or GREEN as shown on a Unit’s profile) are added to the roll for any of their Units In Play with the Tactician Keyword.

Note that the Tactician Keyword may be on some Units that are not Command Units, and these Units will contribute their Command Dice as normal but may not themselves issue orders (see below). A player’s Command Dice may be reduced as the game goes on if they are careless with their Commanders!

Each player rolls all of their Command Dice, and may immediately re-roll one Command Die for each Command Unit they have In Play. After this is done, add up the Power Swords shown on the dice. This is the total number of Command Points each player has available for the Round about to be played (so a die showing two Power Swords means two Command Points for example).

Keep aside the Command Dice you rolled and use them as counters to keep track of how many Command Points you have available that Round.

During a Round, Command Points are spent in a number of ways to increase the utility of an army. Players must either spend all their available Command Points for the Round or lose them. They cannot be saved for future Rounds. As you spend your Command Points, rotate the Command Dice down to the appropriate number to reflect how many Command Points you have spent and that you have left for the Round.

The following Tactical Orders are available to both players during a Round by spending Command Points from their pool. These orders can be used on any friendly unit that is In Play, as it is assumed that they are issued by squad commanders or vehicle squadrons’ commanders, which are imbedded in their unit.

Command Point Cost Order Timing Effect
1 Keep Going! (Extra Activation) After activating a Unit in a Phase and completing its action Activate another Unit before returning play to your opponent to have their turn. A player may only interrupt the normal turn sequence like this once before their opponent must take another turn. This order may not be used with the first player’s first Activation in a Phase (i.e. the player going first in a Phase may not Activate two Units until their opponent has Activated at least one).
1 Fight on! (Re-roll) After rolling to hit or to damage a target

Re-roll up to two dice in a Unit’s roll that failed to hit or damage a target with a Shooting or Assault attack. Remember though that you cannot re-roll any dice that have already been re-rolled for other reasons. You can only do this once per roll against a specific target (with all the involved weapons).

For example, you roll eight dice and roll five misses. You can spend a Command point to re-roll two misses, but you cannot then decide that you are going to re-roll two more misses. You could however, then choose to spend another Command Point to re-roll up to two dice that then failed to damage.

When engaging multiple targets (in multiple assaults or when a unit is allowed to split fire by a special rule, or a Blast Template covers different targets…) you could for example roll three dice against target A, and spend a Command point to re-roll two misses. Then you roll five dice to hit against target B, and you could also spend another Command point to re-roll two misses.
1+ Courage! (Clear Pin marker) In the End Phase (Roll for Pin markers removal step) before any dice are rolled. Each Command point spent removes one Pin marker from one
friendly Unit.

Each faction has Strategic Orders that are unique to their armies. So, for example, the Enforcers have access to different Strategic Orders than the Plague.

Like Tactical Orders, Strategic Orders are special effects that are paid for using Command Points. All Strategic Orders must be declared before any relevant dice are rolled.

Unlike a Tactical Order, a Strategic Order comes from more senior commanders, so unless specified otherwise, it can be used only on friendly Units that are within the Command Radius (in inches) of a friendly Command Unit (as normal, at least one Base needs to be within range). Strategic Orders can be used on the Command Unit itself. Units that are out of the Command Radius of any friendly Command Units, cannot have any Strategic Orders played on them.

If a Command Unit is occupying a building or being transported by a vehicle (as explained in the relevant sections of these rules), measure the Command Radius from the building itself or any of the transport vehicles carrying the Command Unit. Likewise, to issue an order to a Unit inside a transport or a building, the Command Unit must be in range of the transports or the building.

Only one Strategic Order may be used each activation. The Strategic Order may be used before or after, but not during, an action – and each order will specify when it can be used. Most Strategic Orders will affect a single Unit and are resolved immediately, or will affect that Unit’s next action.

For Example: An Enforcer player wants to use the Go, Go, Go! Strategic Order on one of their units with a Sprint Action Token, that is within the 16” Command Radius of an Enforcer Captain. To use this Strategic Order, the player pays the cost of 2 Command Points when the target unit activates. When the Unit has completed its movement, and if it is not engaged in base contact with the enemy, its Sprint Action Token is replaced with a Combat Token.

Sometimes two or more strategic orders, or indeed any other rules, may be triggered at the same time (e.g. when a unit moves within a certain range). If it matters in which order these rules are going to be resolved, then the player with the Initiative Token decides the order in which they are resolved (unless the rules state otherwise)

In the Movement Phase, only Units that have Advance or Sprint Action Tokens may activate and move. Units that have Overwatch Action Tokens are preparing to offer covering, aimed or snap-fire in support of their comrades later (or if they know they may be assaulted so they can fire as a reaction). The player with the Initiative chooses to go first or second. Players then take it in alternating turns to “activate” and move their Units one at a time. Players cannot elect to pass their turn. Once a player runs out of Units to move, the other player finishes moving their remaining Units.

Soldiers in Epic Warpath have been trained to act as part of a team following the directions of their Unit and squad leaders. They must move and fight together. Each Base in a Unit must be within 1” of at least one other Base in the Unit, in an uninterrupted chain or group, and within 6” of all the other Bases in the Unit. This is called Coherency.

Removal of Bases from a Unit (e.g. due to casualties) should be performed to maintain Unit Coherency whenever possible. If any Base from a Unit finds itself outside of Coherency, the first time the Unit moves it must return within Coherency.

To move a Unit, simply measure the distance from the edge of the Bases and move them up to the maximum the Unit can move for the action being performed. This move can be in a straight line, or curved to avoid other models or terrain, and end up facing in any direction. Do make sure that the final positions of all the Bases in the Unit keeps it in Coherency and that no part of any base has moved more than the maximum distance allowed.

When a Unit with an Advance action moves, it may move up to the first of its Speed stat values. So, a Unit with a Speed of 4/8, could move up to 4”.

When a Unit with a Sprint action moves, it may move up to the value of its second Speed stat value. So, a Unit with a Speed of 4/8, could move up to 8”. Only Units with Sprint actions are permitted to engage enemy Bases in an Assault by moving in to base-to-base contact (see below).

A player may elect not to move a Unit at all when it activates.

No Units’ Bases may come within 1” of any enemy Unit unless they are engaging that Unit in an Assault (see below) by moving into base-to-base contact. Such Units are also then permitted to be within 1” of other enemy Units that happen to be in close proximity, while they are engaged. Units can come within 1” of friendly Units so long as they end their move clear of them (see below).

A Unit may move through another, unengaged (not in base-to-base contact with the enemy), friendly Unit as long as its Bases end their moves at least 1” away.

Some very large vehicles can even just turn on their centre point and rotate through Friendly models, so long as they finish any turning clear of other Bases.

In general, friendly Units should, as much as possible, be kept apart, and should never be in base contact with other friendly Units (except where the rules specify otherwise). If you cannot keep friendly Units at least 1” apart, a smaller distance is acceptable, but make sure it is clear to your opponent which Bases belong to which Unit.

s.t: Moving Units off of the Table
s.h: No Unit may move off the table under normal circumstances and must immediately stop at the edge of the table if forced to do so. If permitted to leave the table by Scenario-specific rules then all Bases must be able to reach the table edge during its movement to do so. If a Unit leaves the table, simply remove all the Bases from the Unit and place them off the table, making it clear they have not been destroyed. They are, however, no longer In Play.

A Unit with a Sprint token may move into base-to-base contact with a single enemy Unit, to engage them in an Assault. Simply move each assaulting Base into contact with at least one base in the target unit, contacting unengaged Bases first, so that as many enemy Bases as possible (normal movement rules permitting) are engaged, while still keeping the Assaulting Unit in coherency. Note that Units with the APC keyword cannot move to engage and Assault Units that have an Action Token (see page 46).

While engaged in a multiple combat involving several Units, the 1” rule for keeping Units separate does not apply to the Units involved.

In this example, the Peacekeepers (PK) have a Sprint Action Token and want to move to Assault the Zombies. Each PK Base can move up to 8” when Sprinting, so only three are able to reach and make base contact with as many of the Zombies as they can. The other Bases in the Unit will move as far as they can to try and support the attack while remaining in Coherency.

After engaging the enemy as described above, Assaulting Units swap their Action Token(s) for a Combat Token.

However, if any part of the moving Unit’s movement (even a single Base) was in or through Difficult terrain, or into or from a Building, they are Hindered and their Combat Token is swapped for a Combat (-1) token instead.

Any Unit that is Assaulted and therefore engaged in base-to-base contact by the enemy, swaps any Sprint or Advance tokens it still has for a Combat Token (losing its chance to move!).

If a Vehicle/Walker Unit is assaulted by anything other than another Super-heavy/Vehicle/Walker while they still have an Advance or Sprint Token, they retain their Advance/Sprint Token. When activated, they can move out of base contact with the unit(s) that engaged them. If they can’t (or choose not to) move out of base contact when activated, they swap their Token for a Combat Token.

If a Super-heavy Unit is assaulted by anything other than another Super-heavy Unit while they still have an Advance or Sprint Token, they retain their Advance/Sprint Token. When activated, they can move out of base contact with the unit(s) that engaged them. If they can’t (or choose not to) move out of base contact when activated, they swap their Token for a Combat Token.

If a Unit assaults an enemy Unit that has an Overwatch Token, move the assaulting Bases in as normal, then immediately resolve the Overwatch fire against the assaulting Unit (see page 22), and finally remove the Overwatch Token from the shooting Unit (do not give it a Combat Token). The Unit will still fight the Assault in the Combat Phase, but will not have the chance to trigger the assault when it wants to.

Note however, that weapons with the Blast keyword and weapons with a minimum range (like some artillery) cannot be used to shoot at an engaging enemy in this way. If the Unit being assaulted has no other weapons, swap its Overwatch token for a Combat Token instead and it does not fire (but will have the chance to trigger the assault later itself when it wants). If a Command Unit is Assaulted, it loses any Tokens it has, but immediately resolves any Overwatch Action it still had against the Assaulting Unit as above.

After a Unit activates, removing or swapping tokens as described below helps keep track of which Units each player has activated, and also acts as reminders for future phases and actions.

After a Unit is activated:

  • If it has an Advance Token, swap it for a Combat Token.
  • If it has a Sprint Token, but didn’t engage the enemy in base-to-base contact, simply remove its Token.
  • • If it has a Sprint Token and engaged the enemy in an Assault (base-to-base contact) then swap the Sprint Token for a Combat Token, or a Combat (-1) Token if Hindered, as described above.

Using a Combat (-1) Token is simply a helpful reminder that the Unit was Hindered when making its Sprint into the enemy. Both types of Token are Combat Tokens.

If Command Units move and don’t engage the enemy in base-to-base contact, they discard their Sprint Token, but keep their Overwatch Token. If Command Units assault an enemy unit, they swap both of their Tokens for a Combat Token. If they are assaulted, they lose any Tokens they have, but immediately resolve any Overwatch Action they had against the Assaulting Unit as normal.

In the Overwatch Phase, only Units that have Overwatch Tokens may activate, shooting any ranged weapons they have. The player with the Initiative chooses to go first or second. Players then take it in alternating turns to “activate” and fire with their Units one at a time. Players cannot elect to pass their turn. Once a player runs out of Units to fire with, the other player finishes firing with their remaining Overwatch Units. When a player activates a Unit with an Overwatch token, instead of firing, they may choose to swap the Overwatch Token for a Combat Token to use later and not fire in this phase. A Unit can only fire weapons it has with a Range presented as a number. Weapons with a range of “A” are used in Assaults.

In this example, the Missile Launchers have Range of 20” and roll one Attack Dice per Base in the firing Unit when rolling to hit. The weapons also have the Armour Penetration (1) and Vicious Keywords. This Unit’s Assault weaponry gives 1 Attack Dice per Base, with no additional Keywords.

Summary of Steps

  1. Nominate a target
  2. Check Range and LOS
    1. In Cover?
  3. Determine Number of Dice to Roll
  4. Roll to Hit
  5. Roll to Damage
  6. Roll to Save
  7. Remove Casualties

When a Unit fires, it can select a single enemy Unit to shoot at (Units cannot normally split their fire against multiple targets). The target must be valid however, so players need to check for LOS and Range as follows below. If a target cannot be seen and/or is out of range, a different target must be selected.

The Unit firing its weapons must be able to see its target, and the target must be in range of its weapons. Check LOS for each Base in the firing Unit to Bases in the target Unit. A Base must have partial or Clear LOS to at least one enemy Base to be able to shoot. Next, check the range from Bases that have LOS to the enemy Bases. The range of each weapon a Unit has is listed in its profile. For example, a weapon with a Range of 18”, can shoot at targets up to 18” away, but no further.

Sometimes, things like artillery weapons may have a minimum range. Targets closer than this minimum range cannot then be shot at. For example a weapon listed with a range of 6-40”, cannot shoot at targets that are closer than 6”, or further away than 40”.

If a Unit has more than one weapon option they may fire with all eligible weapons (meaning the target must be in range of that weapon!) against the same enemy unit. Any weapons with a maximum range less than the measured distance are not eligible and cannot fire. Some weapons have two (or more) firing modes on their profile, indicated by a two-line profile each with a * as shown below. Every time the unit fires these weapons, the player chooses which mode to use before resolving the shooting.

In this example, when firing the Heavy Weapons, the Unit can choose either the TAC Autocannons, or the TAC Missile Launchers.

When a Unit fires, check each of its Bases to see which ones are eligible to fire. Some may be out of range or have Blocked LOS to the enemy. Only those Bases with weapons in Range, and that can see at least one enemy Base, may shoot.

Enemy Base X cannot be seen by any of the shooting Unit. Base B cannot see any enemy Bases in the Target Unit.

Enemy Bases Z are out of the firing Unit’s 12” weapons. Base C is out of Range to any of the enemy Bases.

Unless it is a Super-heavy Unit, a Command Unit can only be selected as a target for Shooting (including being intentionally covered by a Blast Template, see page 27) if it is the closest viable target within range and LOS of the shooting Unit.

Often, the enemy target will get the benefit of being In Cover.

When is a target In Cover?

  • Bases wholly within some terrain types will be In Cover (see page 36).
  • Bases partially obscured by terrain or other Units will be In Cover (see page 11).
  • Some special rules or Keywords may mean a Base is In Cover.

If the majority of Bases in the target Unit (even if they are out of range) are In Cover, or out of sight, from the majority of the eligible shooting Bases the whole target Unit is In Cover. Otherwise, there are no additional penalties to shooting.

If it’s not entirely clear whether the target is In Cover, the shooting player rolls a die. On a 5+ the target is not In Cover, on 4 or less it is.

Here, the majority of the target Unit B are partially obscured or cannot be seen by the majority of shooting Unit A. Therefore, target Unit B is In Cover. Only two Bases in Unit B can be seen at all and so are eligible to be hit and take damage.

s.t: 3. Determine Number of Dice to Roll
s.h: Take a number of D8s equal to the number of eligible firing Bases multiplied by the Attack Dice value of the ranged weapons being used. If a Base has multiple ranged weapons, all those in range can be fired. If there are Weapons with different AP values, or Keywords, then dice should be rolled separately for those weapons, or alternatively, use different coloured dice so that both players know which weapons have resulted in a hit.

Roll the dice and apply any relevant modifiers to the results. Any dice that then equal or exceed the Shoot value of the firing Unit, will each result in a hit. Modifiers are cumulative unless specified otherwise.

If, due to modifiers, a player would need to score more than 8 in order to hit, roll anyway, and natural rolls of 8 (regardless of modifiers) are always a successful hit.

Natural rolls of 1 always miss.

Standard Shooting Modifiers

-1 Target is In Cover
-2 Target has the Fly Keyword. (-1 for Super-heavy target).
-1 Target has the Stealthy Keyword
-1 Shooting Unit has a Pin marker

For each hit take a die and roll again. If, due to modifiers or a high Armour value, it is impossible to Achieve the target number, these dice cannot be rolled. In such cases where a target has a high Armour stat, the firing Weapon will need a Keyword like Armour Penetration, to increase its chances of defeating the target’s armour.

For each die that equals or exceeds the Armour value of the target Unit one Base is removed (see below). The AP (Armour Piercing) of weapons that hit will be added to the rolls to damage, improving the chance to damage.

Only a single point of damage can be allocated to a Base to destroy it. If more damage is caused than there are eligible Bases to remove, excess damage is wasted. Natural rolls of 1 always fail to damage. If any other modifiers are applicable, they are cumulative, unless specified otherwise.

Some Units have a Save (n+) value on their profile. This represents supernatural foresight, plain luck, uncanny reflexes, shielding technology, or any other way to evade damage. When a Unit would take damage, roll a D8 for each point of damage potentially suffered. On a score or n or more, that point of damage is cancelled. Finally, allocate any unsaved points of damage as normal onto the Unit’s Bases.

For example, a unit of four Bases with Save (7+) is attacked and would suffer three points of damage. Three save dice are rolled, and one dice rolls 7 or more. Two points of damage are still unsaved, so the unit removes two Bases.

When Bases take damage and are removed, they are considered destroyed. They are removed from the table and are no longer In Play. The player using the Unit suffering casualties chooses which Bases are removed, but only from those that were eligible targets. Bases that were out of LOS from any shooting Bases, or beyond the range of all the firing weapons, cannot normally be removed and so excess damage may be wasted.

If a Unit loses half or more than its current number of Bases from a single shooting attack, it will receive a Pin marker (see page 34).

e.g. A Unit that currently has five Bases will receive a Pin marker if a shooting attack causes three or more to be removed as casualties.

Units with Overwatch Tokens that were engaged by the enemy in base-to-base contact that Round will have used them to fire at the assaulting enemy in the Movement Phase. Otherwise, Units engaged in an Assault cannot fire any ranged weapons. They are far too busy dealing with the immediate enemy at close quarters.

Units cannot fire at any enemy Units engaged in Assault either, nor intentionally cover them with a Blast Template. There is too great a risk of inflicting casualties on their own side.

On the other hand, because of the imposing size of the target, Units are allowed to shoot at enemy Super-heavy Units even when they are engaged in combat. When doing so, non-Blast weapons suffer an additional -1 to hit. Blast weapons can be fired so that they intentionally cover enemy Super-heavy Units, but in this case, they will only hit Super-heavy targets (friend and enemy) – it is assumed they are fired to explode high above any smaller units engaging the Superheavy target.

Some Weapons spread their effects into a wide area, or have shells or other ammunition that explodes. Such weapons have the Blast Keyword and use the 60mm round Blast Templates to show the weapon’s area of effect.

Blast weapons can be fired directly at a target point of the table within range and LOS. If the weapon also has the Indirect keyword, they can alternatively be fired at any target point within range, regardless of whether the shooting Unit can see it or not.

Note that a Unit must have an Overwatch Action Token, and fire in the Overwatch Phase, to fire Indirectly. If only some Bases in the firing unit can see the target point directly, then you must choose whether to fire with the entire unit Indirectly (if they can), or fire directly with the Bases that can see the original target point (before any scatter), while the other Bases hold their fire.

Summary of Steps

Whether a Unit is firing Directly or Indirectly, the steps are the same:

  1. Place First Template
  2. Roll Potential Scatter (Indirect Fire Only)
  3. Place Additional Templates
  4. Roll to Hit
  5. Roll to Damage
  6. Roll to Save
  7. Remove Casualties

Direct Fire: Place a Blast Template, centred on a point on the table one of the firing Unit’s Bases has LOS and range to. In other words, the centre of the Blast Template must be within range and LOS.

Indirect Fire (Overwatch Phase only): Place a Blast Template, centred on a point on the table one of the firing Unit’s Bases has range to (it can be out of LOS). In other words, the centre of the Blast Template must be within range.

If the Unit is firing using Indirect Fire, now roll the Targeting Die (see page 29). If an ‘On Target’ result is rolled, the template lands where intended. If a number is rolled, move the template the distance in inches shown on the die in the direction of the marked point of the die) – the template has “scattered” to here instead. This is then where the first template actually lands (and if it touches the edge of the table, it is removed, together with any other templates that were part of this attack!).

You now add an additional Blast Template for each additional Base in the Unit that is firing. Usually this is just one per Base, but some Weapons may each fire multiple templates. This is indicated on their profile, for example ‘Blast (2)’. The procedure for placing additional templates is as follows, representing the wider, more indiscriminate area of firing Blast weapons.

Roll the Targeting Die for each additional template. If an ‘ON TARGET’ is rolled, place the template anywhere you wish touching edge-to-edge with the first template. Otherwise, ignore the number and simply place the template edge-to-edge with the first template in the direction indicated by the marked die point and relative to the centre of the initial template (as shown in the diagram below). Any template that ends up touching the edge of the table is removed instead. Once all templates are placed, they form the entire area affected by the blast (the “area of effect”). Note that additional templates may end up overlapping each other.

Now determine how many dice you are going to roll against each Unit covered by the templates in the area of effect by counting the number of Bases in each Unit covered fully or partially by at least one template. Thus, if three Bases in a Unit are covered by templates, three dice are rolled for that Unit. Note that regardless of how many templates are over a particular Base, you only roll to try and hit it once. Now roll to hit against each Unit in turn.

Direct Fire: Use the SH value of the firing Unit, and all normal modifiers apply (e.g. if target is In Cover).

Indirect Fire: Use a shoot value of 5+ and normal modifiers apply, except the normal -1 for being In Cover which can be ignored unless the target Bases are inside a building.

All rolls to hit Bases under a Blast Template have the Sustained Attack keyword (Exploding 8! mechanic).

Three Bases have been covered by the Blast Template. The firing weapon has one Attack Die and so two dice are rolled to hit the first Unit and one die against the other.

For each hit scored, roll to damage as normal. Note that only Bases touched by the Blast Template(s) can be hit and take damage. Such Bases may be out of LOS as an exception to the normal casualty removal rule. Note also that if a template scatters onto a Unit, the Unit is considered to have been targeted (is a target of the attack) for any rule purposes.
When a Unit would take damage, roll a D8 for each point of damage potentially suffered. On a score of n or more, that point of damage is cancelled.
Remove any Bases from the Unit that suffer damage as described on page 26.

The Targeting Die has two result types. Their meaning varies slightly whether they are used for placing the initial template (in Indirect Fire,) or the additional templates, as follows.

When placing the first template (Indirect Fire only)

When placing the additional templates

Note that the Targeting Die is used with other rules too, and the results will have similar effects (being accurate or showing a direction and distance).

In this example of Indirect Fire, the Targeting Die has rolled a 3 Arrow result, so the first Template is moved 3” in the direction indicated.

In this example, the Targeting Die has been rolled twice more to show where to place the other templates [2] and [3] in the barrage being fired, touching the first template [1] in the directions indicated. If an ‘On Target’ result is rolled, the player firing the templates chooses where on the edge to place the template.

In the Combat Phase, only Units that have Combat Tokens may activate, making close-combat attacks or shooting any ranged weapons they have. It doesn’t matter which order players resolve their Units’ actions, so the Combat Phase will be a mix of Units firing and others fighting in close combat. If a unit does not currently have a Combat Token, it cannot be activated in this phase. Note that such a Unit will still fight in an Assault if engaged, but will not have the opportunity to activate and trigger that Assault itself. The player with the Initiative chooses to go first or second. Players then take it in alternating turns to activate their Units one at a time. Otherwise, players cannot elect to pass their turn. Once a player runs out of Units to activate, the other player finishes Shooting or Assaulting with their remaining Units.

When an unengaged Unit with a Combat Token activates, it may shoot with any ranged weapons it has. Shooting follows all the rules already outlined previously in the Overwatch Section.

Once a Unit has fired its weapons and the effects are resolved, remove the Combat Token from the shooting Unit. When a player activates a Unit with a Combat Token that is not engaged with the enemy, instead of firing, they may choose to simply do nothing (there may be no valid targets) – simply remove the token as that Unit’s activation

Units that are in base-to-base contact with each other are said to be engaged in an Assault and must fight each other in close combat. When a player activates an engaged Unit with a Combat Token, both that Unit, and the enemy they are in contact with, fight simultaneously. Both players should follow the process below, finally removing any casualties once they are determined for both sides. Units that are engaged but that do not have a Combat Token themselves will still fight in the assault when it is triggered by any other Unit involved.

All engaged Units (with or without Combat Tokens) must have fought by the end of the Round. Players cannot choose not to fight.

Note that while all Bases involved are assumed to fight simultaneously, it is natural and practical for players to take it in turns to roll for their Units’ attacks. The player that triggered the Assault by spending their Combat Token should roll first, including any re-rolls they want to make.

Summary of Steps

  1. All Units involved attack simultaneously.
    1. Allocate attacks.
    2. Roll to Hit.
    3. Roll to Damage.
    4. Roll to Save
  2. Remove casualties.
  3. Determine Winner. Loser takes Nerve tests.
  4. Tidy Up
    1. Separate from Vehicles and Super-heavies.
    2. Units still in contact - Bases Pile-in
    3. OR
    4. No Units in contact - Units consolidate. Winner can Pile-in.
    5. Remove all Combat Tokens.

Not all Bases in the engaged Units may be close enough to fight. Only the following Bases are eligible for attacking in an Assault:

  • Bases that are in base contact with enemy Bases
  • Bases that are within 1” of Bases belonging to the same unit which are in base contact with enemy Bases. These Bases are said to be ‘in support’.

In this example, six Bases of Zombies and five Bases of Peacekeepers are in base contact, or within 1” of those that are to be able to support. All these Bases will roll dice to attack. The Bases marked with a red X are too far away to attack this turn (but could still die later!).

Determine Number of Dice to Roll

Take a number of D8s equal to the number of eligible attacking Bases multiplied by the dice value of the Assault (Range “A”) weapons being used. If there are weapons with different AP values, or Keywords, then dice should be rolled separately for those weapons, or alternatively, use different coloured dice so that both players know which weapons have resulted in a hit.

Roll the dice and apply any relevant modifiers to the results. Any dice that then equal or exceed the Assault value of the fighting Unit, will each result in a hit. Modifiers are cumulative, unless specified otherwise.

If, due to modifiers, a player would need to score more than 8 in order to hit, roll anyway, and natural rolls of 8 always hit.

Natural rolls of 1 always miss.

Standard Assault Modifiers

-1 Unit has a Combat (-1) token
-1 Unit has a Pin marker
-1 Unit arrived from Reserve this Round
-1 Unit disembarked from transports this Round into Assault (see page 42)
+1 Infantry and Heavy Infantry vs APCs (see page 46)

For each hit, take a die and roll again. If, due to modifiers or a high Armour value, it is impossible to Achieve the target number, these dice cannot be rolled. In such cases where a target has a high Armour stat, the attacking Base will need a Keyword like Armour Penetration, to bring the value down.

For each die that equals or exceeds the Armour value of the target Unit one Base is removed (see below). The AP (Armour Piercing) of weapons/Bases that hit will modify the rolls to damage by an amount equal to the AP of the attacking weapon, improving the chance to damage.

Natural rolls of 1 always fail to damage.

If any other modifiers are applicable, they are cumulative, unless specified otherwise.
When a Unit would take damage, roll a D8 for each point of damage potentially suffered. On a score of n or more, that point of damage is cancelled.

When Bases take damage and are removed, they are considered destroyed. They are removed from the table and are no longer In Play. Starting with the player that has the Initiative, both players alternately choose which Bases are removed from their own Units including Bases that were not eligible to attack.

s.t: 3. Determine Winner and take Nerve tests
s.h:
Total up all the Bases removed by both sides (across all units) during the Assault. Exclude any lost Resilience Tokens from this count. If one side caused less than the other, they are the Loser. The other side is the Winner. Otherwise it is a draw. Note that if one side is completely wiped out in combat, they are the Loser, regardless of the number of casualties they caused!

All Units that were involved and on the losing side are given a Pin marker. The Loser, if they have any Units with Bases remaining, must now take a number of Nerve tests equal to the difference their side lost the combat by. For every failed Nerve test, the Loser must immediately remove a Base from any of their Units involved in the fight (no need to roll for damage, no Saves, no Resilience, etc.).

Firstly, if any Bases are still in base-contact with any Vehicles or Super-heavy Bases, separate them by 1”, with non-Vehicle and non-Super-heavy Bases moving first (unless they are also in contact with another non-Vehicle or non-Super-heavy base, in which case they do not move at all). If both sides have Vehicle or Super-heavy units in the combat, the side with initiative retreats theirs first. If neither Base can move enough to create a 1” gap, they stay engaged. This means in most situations, vehicles and Super-heavy Units will end the Round unengaged.

Now, if any Units still have Bases that remain in contact with each other, starting with the player with the Initiative, players move (Pile-in) any Bases from the engaged Units that are not currently in base contact with the enemy Unit, into base contact. This follows the normal movement rules, even if this would take them further than their normal Speed. A Pile-in move like this cannot be used to engage Vehicle or Super-heavy Units which previously separated from the Assault. Once Pilein moves have been completed, the Assault will then continue next Round.

Or, if a Unit no longer has any Bases in contact with the enemy, that Unit may now make a “consolidation” move up to 3”, following the normal movement rules. If this applies to both players, the Winning player (or the one with the Initiative if there was no Winner) may choose to go first or second. If the Winner goes first, they may choose instead to move their Units back into basecontact with the Loser’s Units (see Pile-in above), to continue the Assault next turn. Otherwise, Units should be separated as per the normal minimum distances (i.e. 1” for both Friendly Units and Enemy Units). A consolidation move therefore cannot be used to move to engage a new enemy Unit. Finally, remove any Combat Tokens from all the Units involved in the fight.
Units that are still engaged will continue to fight in the next Combat Phase. Instead of an Action Token, they will each receive a Combat Token at the start of the next Round.

Some Assaults will involve more than two Units. In such cases, the rules remain the same – all participants from all Units that are in base contact with each other will fight simultaneously.

Any Base that is in base contact with multiple enemy Units may choose which to allocate all its attack dice to.

If a base is in contact with just one of the enemy units, it must direct its attacks against that unit. Bases that are in support can always choose to allocate their attacks against ANY enemy unit their unit is engaged with, regardless of their position. Make it clear to your opponent, which attacks are being allocated where.

The Assault Enforcer Unit (AE) is engaged with the Zombie Unit (ZM). Base E must allocate its attacks to the Zombies as it is only in base-contact with them. The supporting Base F must also allocate its attacks to the Zombies, as its Unit is not engaged with any others, even though it is a multiple combat. The Peacekeeper Unit (PK) is engaged with both the Zombies and the Ghouls (GH). Base B must allocate its attacks to the Zombies as it is not in base-contact with any other Units. Base A may choose which of the two enemy units it is engaged with to allocate its attacks. The supporting bases C and D can also allocate their attacks to either of the enemy units that their unit is engaged with (the Ghouls or the Zombies).

Some weapons or rules will place a Pin marker on a Unit. A Unit can have a maximum of one Pin marker on it.

While a Unit has a Pin marker, it suffers an additional -1 to-hit modifier both for Shooting and for Assault. In addition, if a Unit starts a Round with a Pin marker, it must be given an Advance Token. Also, while a Unit with US 2 or more has a Pin marker, its US counts as 1. A Unit will gain a Pin marker in the following circumstances:

  • A Unit loses half or more of its current number of Bases from a single shooting attack.
  • A Unit loses an Assault.
  • A Unit is hit by any weapons with the Pinning Keyword, even if no casualties are suffered.
  • Bases in a Unit survive being in a destroyed transport vehicle.
  • Remember that Pin markers can be removed during the End Phase.

Once all Combat Tokens have been spent in the Combat phase, no unit should have any Action or Combat Token left. It is time to move to the End Phase, during which you need to work your way through the following steps.
Any special rules with effects that take place in the End Phase are carried out now.

Players take a Nerve test for each of their Units with a Pin marker. If the test is passed, the Pin marker is removed. Command Units, and Units within Command radius of a friendly Command Unit, each roll two dice for these tests and choose the highest.

Players will add any Victory Points to their running total at this point in the End Phase. Players then check the Scenario conditions to see if someone has achieved victory. If not, turn over any Dynamic Objective markers on the table to their other side (so active becomes inactive, and vice versa). The game then continues and the next Round starts with the Command Phase.

At this point, players must remove any tokens/markers that show that a unit is under the effects of a rule that ‘lasts until the end of the Round’. Unless differently specified in a special rule, the only markers/tokens left on the table should be any Pin markers that Units failed to clear.

The battlefields of the future are littered with opportunities to use terrain to stay alive. Terrain can also hinder movement and provide safe blocking features, sheltering your troops from enemy fire. Not all terrain affects infantry and vehicles in the same way. What may be merely difficult for one Unit to move through, may be impassable for another.
Units inside terrain features such as ruins, or craters, can see and be seen, LOS is not affected.

Because of the dense foliage, LOS to and from Bases in a wood is Blocked if it goes through more than 2” of wood. If LOS goes though 2” or less of wood, the target is partially obscured and therefore is automatically in cover. It follows that the ideal position for a base in a wood is to be wholly inside the wood and in contact with the edge of the wood. That means that the base will be able to shoot out of the wood without conferring cover to its targets, as long as LOS is measured from the point where the base touches the wood (see diagram).

Three of the Bases from the Unit of Ghouls are on the edge of the wood and so can see, and draw LOS clear of the wood from those points. All the Bases of the HMGs Unit are entirely within the wood and cannot do this, therefore all of their targets will benefit from cover, and some may not be have LOS at all if there is more than 2” of wood in the way.

Some suggested Terrain Heights are as follows. For comparison, keep in mind that a man-sized unit is Height 2, while tanks and most other vehicles are Height 3.

Type Height
Broken ground / crater 0
Hill 3
Marsh/River 0
Wood 4
Low height building 4
Medium height building 6
Tall building 8
Wall/hedge/fence/ barricade 1

Terrain can block LOS to any Bases behind it in the same way as a Unit. For example, a Height 3 or higher hill will block LOS between two Bases of Height 3 or less. Some terrain pieces such as rivers will be flat (Height 0) and so never block LOS.

If a Unit is positioned on (not in) terrain (e.g. a hill), then add the height of the terrain to the height of the Unit when determining LOS (e.g. on a hill). While a Unit is occupying a building then it has the Height of that building.

Example: a Unit of Height 2 will determine LOS using a Height of 5 when standing on a Height 3 hill. The same Unit occupying a Medium height building will have a Height of 6.
The normal battlefield may have small undulations or debris across it but it does not impact on a Unit’s movement. Unless specified otherwise, all battlefield areas are Open terrain by default.

If a terrain feature is Difficult for a Unit to move through, its movement is restricted. Even if Sprinting, a Unit can only move up to the first of its Speed values (Advance Speed), if any part of the move starts, ends or goes through the Difficult Terrain.
If a terrain feature is Impassable for a Unit, it cannot be moved into or through.

How different terrain elements, typically found on most Epic Warpath tables, affect the different Unit Types is detailed below.

Broken Ground/Rubble/Craters: Height 0
Non-vehicle and non-Super-heavy Bases wholly inside this feature are always In Cover.
Infantry/Heavy Infantry/Walkers/Super-heavy: Open
Bikes/Vehicles: Difficult

Roads: Height 0
Vehicle and Bike Units making their entire Move along a road, can add up to 3” extra to an Advance move and up to 6” extra to a Sprint move.
All Units: Open

Ruins: Height 4
Non-Super-heavy Bases wholly inside this feature are always In Cover.
Infantry/Heavy Infantry/Walkers: Open
Bikes/Vehicles/Super-heavy: Difficult

Marsh/River: Height 0
Infantry/Heavy Infantry/Walkers/ Super-heavy: Difficult
Bikes/Vehicles: Impassable

Low Wall/Hedge/Barricade: Height 1
Infantry/Heavy Infantry/Super-heavy: Open
Bikes/Walkers/Vehicles: Difficult
Bases in contact with this terrain may ignore it when drawing LOS to targets.

High Wall/ Barricade: Height 2
Super-heavy: Open
Infantry/Heavy Infantry/ Walkers: Difficult
Bikes/Vehicles: Impassable

Hill: Height 3
All Unit types treat hills as Open.

Woods: Height 4
Bases wholly inside this feature are always In Cover.
Infantry/Heavy Infantry: Open
Bikes/Walkers/Vehicles/Super-heavy: Difficult
LOS is blocked if it goes through over 2” of wood, and if LOS goes though 2” or less of wood, the target is automatically in cover.

Intact Building: Height 4 or more
Bases wholly inside this feature are always In Cover.
Infantry/Heavy Infantry/Walkers: Open
Bikes/Vehicles/Super-heavy: Impassable
Low level buildings (e.g. a warehouse or small office building) should be Height 4. Taller buildings should be Height 6 or more.

Only Units and Bases of type Infantry, Heavy Infantry and Walker may enter buildings (any transport Vehicles must remain outside!). A building may only contain a single unit at a time, and it may only contain a certain number of Bases. This is the building’s Capacity and it is normally equal to three Bases for each 2” square parts of building (see diagrams below). It is best if you agree with your opponent at the start of the game what the capacity of each building on the table is going to be.

This building has roughly two 2”x2” parts and so has Capacity (6).

This building has roughly three 2”x2” parts, so has Capacity (9).

In order to enter a building, all Bases in the Unit must have enough movement to reach the building. If not all the Bases in a Unit have the movement to reach the building (or the building does not have enough Capacity for the Unit), the whole Unit must remain outside.

If all the Bases reach the building, then the Unit is placed on the building roof where possible, with any Bases that don’t fit being put off the table to one side. The unit is now occupying the building. From that point on, all ranges and Line of Sight for the unit are measured to/from the building itself, as if the footprint of the building was the footprint of the occupying Unit. All Bases inside the building are assumed to be both visible and able to see out of the building.

To leave a building in later Rounds, a Unit must be given a Sprint or Advance action. A Unit cannot enter and leave the same building in the same Round, unless it is to move to an adjacent section in a large building (see page 40).

While occupying buildings, Units have the Height of the building. They are In Cover and have +1 Armour when shot at. For example, a Unit with an Armour value of 5+, would have it increased to 6+ while in a building.

If the unit inside a building is hit by a weapon with the Demolisher Keyword, there is chance the building might also collapse. Before resolving the hits on the unit in the building, roll a single die to damage the building itself. Buildings have an AR of 9+. If a building is destroyed, replace it with a Ruins terrain element in the same footprint (of a Height equal to half the Height of the building). Any Bases that were occupying the building are immediately destroyed (with no chance to use Saves or Resilience tokens or anything else). If the building is not destroyed, then proceed with resolving the hits against the target unit. Units with Demolisher weapons can also deliberately target unoccupied buildings with their Shooting attacks. If they score at least one hit on the building, roll a single die to damage the building as described above.

If any Blast Template from a shooting attack has its centre point on the building, the shell has hit the building and all Bases in the building are considered to be covered by the template. If a Blast Template is not centred on the building but touches the building, then just one of the Bases in the building is considered to be covered by the template for each template touching the building (up to a maximum of the number of Bases in the building). In either case, Bases outside buildings that are under templates can still be hit as normal.

In this example, the building has been touched by two of the Blast Templates, so two Bases are considered covered by the area of effect (or a single Base if the Unit consisted of a single Base).

A Unit cannot move into an enemy-occupied building. It must Assault from outside the building instead. If a Unit Assaults a Unit in a building, the attack is always Hindered. Assaulting Bases are moved into base-to-base contact with the building itself to count for the following combat and are then considered Engaged with the Unit inside.

Bikes may Assault buildings but cannot enter them, and suffer an additional -1 to hit modifier in the Assault, as well as being Hindered. Vehicles cannot Assault Units in buildings.

All Bases in the building, and all Bases in contact with it (plus assaulting Bases in support position of those in base contact with the building) fight in the ensuing Assault. Bases may allocate their attacks to any enemy Units involved. Declare how all units allocate attacks before resolving any unit’s attacks. If the occupying Unit loses, any Nerve tests it must then take have a +2 modifier.

If, after any Nerve tests are taken, the attackers wipe out all occupying defenders, any surviving attackers may move into the building as a consolidation move (if the building is not Impassable to them and if they can all fit!). If they don’t fit in the building, they can make a normal consolidation move outside the building instead. Otherwise, the occupying unit remains in place and the attacking Unit(s) remain at the base of the building. Super-Heavy Units will separate as normal.

For both ongoing and multiple assaults, attacks allocated against the Unit occupying the building will still be Hindered. Use a Combat (-1) token as a reminder, but the -1 for being Hindered will not actually apply if any attacks are allocated to other Units outside the building (unless the Unit has been Hindered generally for some other reason!).

A Unit with Assault Demolisher weapons can deliberately target any building (occupied or not) it is in base contact with, in an Assault. The Unit must allocate all its Assault attacks to the building, but has a +1 modifier to hit it. If the Unit scores at least one hit on the building with a weapon with the Demolisher keyword, roll a single die to damage the building as described in the shooting section above. Any Bases subsequently destroyed inside the building will count towards determining the Winner/Loser of the Assault.

Sometime, you may wish to split larger buildings into connected sections, each with its own Capacity. Treat each section as its own building for the purposes of moving, LOS and shooting. If a unit moves from one section to another adjacent one, it can do so with an Advance or Sprint action. If the section is occupied, it must fight a Hindered Assault as normal against the enemy Unit in the adjacent section, but remains in its own section if it fails to destroy the enemy Unit.

A Unit can shoot at an enemy Unit in an adjacent section, following the normal rules for firing at units in buildings. A particularly tall building could potentially be split into sections. This requires some discussion between the players however, but a Unit occupying a section would still have the Height of that section.

In this example, the building has roughly five 2”x2” parts, and one area of the building model is much taller. The players decide the split the building into two sections.

The shorter Height 4 (blue) area is declared a section with Capacity (9) while the taller Height 6 (red) area is declared a section with Capacity (6).

Some Vehicles may transport other Friendly Units. Such Units will have a Capacity(n) listed for them, where (n) is the number of Bases each Vehicle in the Unit can carry. Unless specified otherwise, only friendly Infantry or Heavy Infantry Bases can be carried in Units with a Capacity(n).

A Unit of transport vehicles can normally only carry a single friendly Unit (no mixed Units being transported). Likewise, a Unit cannot be embarked within more than one transport Unit. The transport vehicle Unit and the transported Unit are assigned a single Action Token. If you need to measure the range to a Unit that is being transported, measure the range to the closest of their transports.
Entering and Leaving Transport Vehicles Units cannot both enter and exit transport vehicles in the same Round.

When a unit moves to enter a transport vehicles unit, simply measure to the base of any of the vehicles. If not all the Bases in a Unit can reach a vehicle the whole Unit must remain outside. If all the Bases reach a vehicle, then the unit is removed from the table and set aside. It is assumed they are inside the vehicles. After troops have entered transport vehicles, the vehicles are free to activate and move as normal.

Units in a vehicle cannot shoot or be shot at, and they cannot be Assaulted directly. Of course, the vehicles themselves can still be shot at or Assaulted as normal.

If a unit of loaded transports takes damage from ranged attacks and loses vehicles, the transported unit takes a number of hits equal to the number of destroyed transports multiplied by their Capacity. Roll to damage the transported unit as normal, with no AP modifier or any other rule or modifier – just a straight roll against their Armour.

If after resolving these hits the transport Unit no longer has enough total Capacity to carry the remaining Bases in the transported unit, you have two choices.

The first option is to remove enough Bases from the transported unit to ensure the Unit still fits into the remaining transports (the removed Bases count as destroyed unfortunately, but you can imagine they are retreating back to base!).

The second option is for the Unit to immediately make an emergency disembarkation - place all remaining transported Bases in contact with the surviving transports, or as much as possible within the footprint of the transport vehicles if the transport unit has been wiped out. If some of the transported Bases cannot be placed as described above because of physical constrains like impassable terrain or enemy units (which they must be able to be at least 1” away from), these Bases are destroyed – they were trapped in the burning wrecks of their transports. Finally, place a Pin marker on the disembarked unit and discard any Token they (and their transports) had.

For example, a Unit of four transports (Capacity 2) are transporting a unit of Infantry made of seven Bases. The transports are shot at and lose two vehicles. The transported Unit takes four hits (i.e. two destroyed vehicles with Capacity 2 each). The enemy rolls to damage and destroys two transported Bases. The unit has now five Bases in a transport unit with total Capacity of 4. The player can decide to either remove one more Base and carry on, or the remaining five bases must leave the transports immediately, as described above.

If a transport Unit is assaulted and engaged by an enemy Unit and the Unit inside can still activate (even if it has an Overwatch Action Token, although it will not get to shoot), when it does so, it has two choices. It can either remain inside the vehicles, or it can counter-assault the enemy Unit(s) that have assaulted the vehicles. If the Unit decides to counter-assault, then as many of its Bases as possible are placed directly into base contact anywhere with the enemy Bases that assaulted the vehicles, or into support position if there is no space for base contact. Give the Unit a -1 Combat Token for disembarking from the vehicle into Assault (it can no longer activate in the Movement Phase). If there is not enough room for all of the embarked Bases to get out in this way, the Unit must remain onboard, unactivated.

If the transported Unit has already activated or has remained onboard, and the loaded transports then take damage in an assault, first resolve the assault completely, including consolidation moves. Then roll for the damage on transported Units caused by their transports being destroyed (both by enemy attacks and by failed Nerve tests!). Finally, if the transported unit no longer fits in the remaining transports, it must make an emergency disembarkation, or lose the surplus Bases, as described above.

For example, a unit of four transports (Capacity 2) are transporting a unit of Infantry made of seven Bases. The transports are assaulted and lose two vehicles to enemy attack. They lose the combat and then lose another transport to a failed Nerve test. The transported unit takes six hits (i.e. three destroyed vehicles with Capacity 2 each). The enemy rolls to damage and destroys three transported Bases. The unit has now four Bases in a transport unit with total Capacity of 2. The player can remove two further Bases, or the remaining four Bases must immediately make an emergency disembarkation from the remaining transport, as described above.

If a Unit activates and leaves its transport before the vehicles move, the vehicles are free to move in their own activation as they wish. Simply leave the Action Token with the vehicle Unit to spend later.

If the transport vehicles activate and move before the troops inside activate, the vehicle receives a Combat Token as normal. The transported unit may immediately activate for free once the vehicles’ action is complete, in order to disembark as below. Alternatively, the transported unit may choose to remain inside the vehicles and wait to activate and disembark later, in which case leave the Action Token next to the vehicles, together with their Combat Token. This shows that the Combat Token applies to the vehicles, while the Action Token applies to the transported unit.

When disembarking, if the transport vehicles moved using an Advance action, the troops inside may subsequently leave and Advance as normal. If the transport vehicles moved using a Sprint action, the troops inside may not disembark if the vehicles moved more than their Advance Speed value. Otherwise, they may disembark and make their Sprint move, but only as far as their own Advance Speed value. They are still permitted to engage enemy Units in an Assault, but will have a Combat (-1) token for doing so. If an assaulting unit disembarking from a transport would be Hindered by terrain or other effects too, then they receive a second Combat (-1) token and will suffer a total of -2 modifier on their rolls to hit. Double Hindrance!

To leave a transport, in either case, simply measure the move of the Bases from the vehicle they are leaving (up to a maximum of n Bases per vehicle), ending the move in Coherency, as normal. If the Unit of vehicles had a Pin marker, place a Pin marker on the disembarked Unit too. In either case, place Combat Tokens on both the vehicle and troops Units if appropriate.

If a transport Unit assaults an enemy Unit that has an Overwatch action, resolve the Overwatch fire after any transported Unit disembarks for free. Assuming the transported Unit also assaults the Unit with Overwatch, the Overwatch fire may be resolved against either attacking Unit (vehicles or troops), otherwise it is resolved as normal.

If a Unit of Transport Vehicles receives a Pin marker, any Unit inside will also receive a Pin marker. If a Unit with a Pin marker boards a Transport Vehicle Unit, it may immediately make a free Nerve test to remove the Pin marker, just like in the End Phase (so proximity to a Command Unit will help too). If they fail, they keep the Pin marker until they can next try to shake it off.

Sometimes, Command Units are transported inside a Vehicle. While the Command Unit is embarked, the transport Unit is also considered a Command Unit, for the purposes of receiving Action Tokens and being targeted. As soon as a Command Unit leaves a transport, the transport Unit reverts to its normal non Command status (although keeps any Action Token it still has to use this Round).

Sometimes, a Command Unit will have a Capacity and can therefore transport other, non-Command Units. As a Command Unit, it will receive both a Overwatch and a Sprint token when action tokens are assigned. Any non-Command Units transported inside, may each select either a Sprint or Advance action token, rather than getting the same as the transport as normal.

Units with the Fly Keyword are mounted on round flying bases. They operate above the battlefield and suffer less restriction of movement than their counterparts on the ground. They have a larger Coherency than usual and must remain with 3” of Bases in the same Unit, instead of the normal 1”.
